followUps:
No. Hooks only work inside function components and other hooks, so a class component cannot call them directly.

If you have a class that needs a hook, wrap the hook in a small function component and pass the result down (as a prop or a render prop), or convert the class. Both styles can live in the same app: classes keep working and nothing forces you to rewrite them. Error boundaries still need a class today.

Rule 1: call hooks only at the top level (no ifs, loops or nested functions). Rule 2: call them only from function components or custom hooks. They exist because React finds each hook's data by call order, not by name.

Example: if render 1 calls useState, useEffect, useState and render 2 skips the effect, the second useState reads the effect's slot. Same order every render means every call meets its own data.

code.title: State is a snapshot: plain value vs updater

followUps:
Pass a plain value when the new value does not depend on the old one, such as setName(e.target.value), setOpen(false) or resetting a form to its initial value.

The value is the whole intent there, so reading the current snapshot is fine. Use the updater form only when the result is computed from the previous state, like counters, toggles (setOn(o => !o)) or appending to a list.

The result is 6 if count was 0 and the handler is setCount(5); setCount(c => c + 1): 6. React applies the queue in order, so 5 is set first, then the updater gets 5 and returns 6.

Reverse the order, setCount(c => c + 1); setCount(5), and the final value is 5, because the last plain value overwrites the earlier result. Think of each call as an item in a queue.

code.title: useEffect: deps, cleanup order, unmount

followUps:
Because a new object or array is a different reference on every render, and Object.is compares references, not contents. {page: 1} built during render is never equal to the one from the last render.

So the effect looks "changed" every time and re-runs. Fixes: depend on primitives (page), build the object inside the effect, or keep a stable reference with useMemo or by moving it outside the component.

useEffect runs after the browser has painted; useLayoutEffect runs after React updates the DOM but before the paint. Prefer useEffect.

Use useLayoutEffect only when you must measure the DOM and change something before the user sees it, for example reading an element's height to position a tooltip. It blocks painting, so slow work there makes the page feel janky. Both take the same arguments and use the same cleanup rules.

code.title: Conditional hook shifts the slots

followUps:
It does not detect them by running anything: the plugin reads the source text and treats any call to a function named use followed by a capital letter (or use itself) as a hook call.

It then checks where the call sits. A hook inside an if, a loop, after an early return or in a nested function is reported. The name rule is why hooks must start with "use": a function named fetchStuff that calls useState would not be understood as a hook.

Not exactly. use() is the one hook-like API that may be called inside conditions and loops, because it reads a promise or context without relying on a slot per call.

It still has to be called while rendering, in a component or a custom hook, not in event handlers or effects. Example: if (show) { const data = use(promise); } is allowed, while if (show) useState(0) is not.

code.title: Stale closure and three fixes

followUps:
A stale value is desired when you want "the value at the moment of the event", like a handler that logs or submits the form data exactly as it was rendered.

Example: a user clicks "Send" and a 3 second delayed confirmation should show the message that was sent, not whatever they typed in the meantime. Snapshots make that natural. A stale value only becomes a bug when a long-lived callback should see the latest value.

First log the value inside the long-lived callback and compare it with what the screen shows; if they differ, you have a stale closure. Then check the effect's dependency list: the lint rule react-hooks/exhaustive-deps flags most cases.

Quick test: change the code to an updater (setCount(c => c + 1)) or read ref.current; if the bug disappears, the closure was the cause. Also look for a [] that hides a dependency.

React sets ref.current to the DOM node during the commit phase, after the DOM has been created or updated, and sets it back to null when the element is removed.

So refs are empty during the first render and usable in effects and event handlers. Reading inputRef.current.focus() inside useEffect works; doing it in the render body would find null on mount. A callback ref runs at the same moments.

In React 18 a function component could not take ref as a normal prop: you wrapped the child in forwardRef((props, ref) => ...). In React 19 ref is an ordinary prop, so the child just reads props.ref.

// React 19
function Input({ ref, ...rest }) {
  return <input ref={ref} {...rest} />;
}

forwardRef still works but is no longer needed.

code.title: React.memo: shallow props compare and identity

followUps:
No. It is a performance hint, not a guarantee. React may throw away cached values, for example to free memory or while a component is offscreen, and recompute them later.

Write code that is still correct if the function runs again: no side effects inside it, and never use it for something that must run exactly once. Dependencies changing always forces recalculation, so useMemo(() => sort(list), [list]) recomputes whenever list is a new array.

By default it compares each prop with Object.is, one level deep (shallow). Numbers and strings are equal by value; objects, arrays and functions only if they are the same reference.

You can pass a second argument: memo(Comp, (prev, next) => prev.id === next.id) returns true when the props count as equal and the render can be skipped. Use it sparingly, since a wrong comparison hides updates.

code.title: Pure reducer for a fetch lifecycle

followUps:
Model it as a state object with a status field (idle, loading, success, error) plus data and error, and use three actions: start, success, fail.

case 'start':   return { status: 'loading', data: null, error: null };
case 'success': return { status: 'success', data: a.data, error: null };
case 'fail':    return { status: 'error', data: null, error: a.error };

This makes impossible mixes (loading and error at once) unrepresentable, and each transition is easy to unit test.

The reducer stays synchronous and pure; async work happens outside it and then dispatches the outcome.

Steps: in an event handler or effect, dispatch start, run await fetch(...), then dispatch success or fail. Because dispatch has a stable identity, it can sit in a dependency array without causing re-runs. Libraries like Redux Toolkit wrap this pattern as thunks.

Pass a plain value when you only need to overwrite.

Wait, the question here is how to test the hook: use fake timers. Render the hook with a test utility such as renderHook, change the value, advance time by less than the delay (value unchanged), then advance past it (value updated). Also unmount before the delay and check nothing fires. With 300 ms delay: advance 299 ms, expect the old value; advance 1 more, expect the new one.

Debounce waits until the user stops, then fires once; throttle fires at a steady rate while the user keeps going.

Use debounce for search-as-you-type or auto-saving after typing stops: typing 10 letters quickly gives 1 call. Use throttle for scroll, resize and drag handlers: with a 100 ms throttle, 1 second of scrolling gives about 10 calls. Debounce suits "final value" needs, throttle suits "keep updating".

code.title: useDebounce logic with a fake clock

followUps:
Test it with fake timers so no test waits for real time. Render the hook with a test utility such as renderHook, change the value, then move the clock.

Steps: advance 299 ms and expect the old value; advance 1 more ms and expect the new value; change the value twice quickly and expect only the last one to arrive; unmount before the delay and expect no state update and no warning. With a 300 ms delay those four checks cover the whole behavior.

Strict Mode mounts, unmounts and mounts every component once in development, so an effect runs setup, cleanup, setup. A missing abort or an effect that is not repeatable shows up at once, as duplicate requests.

It does not create the flood loop itself, but it makes you see the first duplicate early. You will see two requests on mount in the Network tab and, if cleanup is missing, both responses may update state. Aborting in cleanup makes the first request cancel.

code.title: Object in deps re-runs the effect every render

followUps:
Add useRef by storing a slot holding { current: init } that is created once and returned unchanged every render. useMemo and useCallback store { value, deps } and recompute only when deps differ.

function useMemo(fn, deps) {
  const slot = nextSlot(() => ({ deps: null, value: null }));
  if (!slot.deps || changed(slot.deps, deps)) { slot.value = fn(); slot.deps = deps; }
  return slot.value;
}
// useCallback(f, d) = useMemo(() => f, d)

Layout effects run synchronously right after the DOM changes, before the browser paints. Passive effects (useEffect) are scheduled to run later, after paint, so they never block the screen.

In a from-scratch version, keep two lists: after the render, flush the layout list immediately, then schedule the passive list with setTimeout or MessageChannel. A state update inside a layout effect triggers a synchronous re-render before the user sees the first one.

code.title: useState and useEffect from scratch

followUps:
Strict Mode only runs the extra mount and unmount in development, so analytics sent in an effect looks doubled there but fires once in production. Do not hack around it with a "ran already" flag.

Better: send the event from the user action itself (click handler), or make it idempotent with an id so the server ignores duplicates. For "page viewed", a module-level variable keyed by page works, or let the analytics library de-duplicate. Accept the double call in development.

Activity (formerly Offscreen) lets React hide part of the UI while keeping its state, for example a tab you left. When hidden, its effects are cleaned up; when shown again, they are set up again.

That is the same cleanup-and-setup cycle Strict Mode simulates, which is why effects must be symmetric. Example: a hidden chat tab should unsubscribe from its socket on hide and resubscribe on show, while the typed draft text stays in state.

code.title: Strict Mode double mount exposes a missing cleanup

followUps:
Measure first, then change one thing at a time. Use the Profiler to find which components re-render and why, and note which context causes it.

Steps: (1) split the big context into a state context and a dispatch context, or by update frequency; (2) memoize the provider value; (3) move rarely used data out; (4) for hot data (many consumers, partial reads) move to a store with selectors such as Zustand. Re-measure after each step; stop when the slow interaction is acceptable.

Server Components fetch and render on the server, so a lot of data no longer needs client state at all: it arrives as props or via async components. Less global client state is needed.

What remains on the client is interactive state (forms, UI toggles, optimistic updates). Context still works, but only inside Client Components, and a provider can wrap server-rendered children passed as children. So the question often shrinks to small client stores.

The compiler skips (bails out of optimizing) a component when it breaks the Rules of React: mutating props or state, writing to a ref during render, reading mutable values from outside, or calling hooks conditionally.

Example: props.items.push(x) or ref.current = value in the render body. The ESLint integration reports these. Components it skips still run correctly, they just do not get automatic memoization, so fix the impure code to benefit.

Keep the typed text in normal state so the input updates at once, and pass it through useDeferredValue: const deferred = useDeferredValue(query). Filter the big list with deferred.

React renders the urgent update first and then the list with the old value in the background, and drops that work if you type again. Unlike debounce there is no fixed delay: on a fast machine the list updates almost instantly, and no network call is delayed. Wrap the list in memo so the deferred render is skipped when unchanged.
